what_this_measures: Cross-script RETRIEVAL recall, before the D-A/D5 re-embed. For each sampled toponym, a partner is a DIFFERENT toponym attesting one of the same place_ids — so the ground truth is co-attestation, not a hand-typed list.

In practice the partners are the romanisation of the query (Thai script -> Latin transliteration). That is the realistic query shape for Thai, and a much harder task than same-script variant matching. Absolute recall is therefore low by nature.

🛑 A AND B ARE NOT EQUIVALENT AT BASELINE. Group A (NFKC-affected) is already about 3.5x harder to retrieve than group B at R@200, with a median rank of 438 against 168. So a post-re-embed test of 'is A now worse than B' is CONFOUNDED. The valid test is difference-in-differences: how much each group MOVES, not where each ends up.

🛑 GROUP C IS NOT A CONTROL FOR A. Its partners are same-script case/accent variants (French 'Ecole'/'école'), an easier task entirely. B is A's control: same script, same pair type, differing only in whether NFKC touches the name. C is context only.

⚠ GROUP A SATURATES AT 714 of a requested 1,000, with the sampler widened from 12 to 40 random-seed passes. That is the accessible population of NFKC-affected Thai names carrying a co-attested partner, not a sampler shortfall. Its denominator is 685 paired.

⚠ The query document is excluded from its own KNN ranking. Counting it made R@1 structurally 0.0000 in every group and inflated every rank by one; an earlier run of this harness had that defect and its numbers must not be mixed with these.

This measures retrieval, not embedding drift — it is the SIGNED measurement that the drift baseline (76519ef) explicitly cannot provide, and that §55.3 names as the condition that would reopen the Thai normalisation decision.
how_to_compare: Re-run this harness unchanged after the re-embed against the same recorded ids. Compute delta R@k and delta median rank per group. Test A's delta against B's delta. A regression is A falling further than B; A and B falling together is a corpus-wide effect, not a Thai one.
